standard: Subscription / SaaS churn & retention metrics corpus

entries.title: Logo (customer) churn rate
entries.body: Logo churn = number of customers who cancelled ÷ total customers at start of period. Measures how many customers leave regardless of size. Most relevant for SMB-focused SaaS where each customer is a similar revenue slice.

entries.title: Revenue (MRR/dollar) churn rate
entries.body: Revenue churn = MRR lost from cancellations and downgrades ÷ total MRR at start of period. Weighted by customer size. A few large churners show low logo churn but high revenue churn — the two must be tracked separately.

entries.title: Monthly churn benchmarks — industry context
entries.body: Under 1%/month is excellent; 1–2% good; 2–5% concerning for most models; above 5%/month is critical — at 5% monthly, half the customer base turns over in ~14 months, making sustainable growth very difficult.

entries.title: Churn benchmarks by ARR stage (ChartMogul)
entries.body: Median early-stage SaaS: 6.2% net MRR churn / 4.1% gross. Over $1M ARR: 2.3% net / 5.3% gross. Over $15M ARR: 1.8% net / 5.8% gross. Churn compresses as companies find product-market fit and sharpen their customer category.

entries.title: Gross vs net churn — net includes expansion
entries.body: Net churn subtracts expansion revenue; gross churn does not. A business can show low gross churn but high net churn if expansion is masking leakage, or vice versa. Always report both to read true retention quality.

entries.title: 30–50% of total churn happens in first 90 days
entries.body: Most churn occurs before the customer reaches their 'aha moment'. Onboarding is the highest-leverage churn intervention: improve activation and the first-90-day experience to cut lifetime churn materially.

entries.title: Involuntary churn — ~11% revenue lost to payment failures
entries.body: About 11% of subscription revenue is lost annually to involuntary churn (expired cards, insufficient funds, fraud blocks). Smart-retry / dunning systems recover roughly 70% of these failures — a high-ROI retention lever often overlooked.

entries.title: Track churn on monthly cohort basis
entries.body: Monitor logo and revenue churn on a monthly cohort (or weekly at high volume) basis rather than a single annual number. Cohort curves reveal whether retention is improving and where in the lifecycle leakage concentrates.

entries.title: High logo churn + low revenue churn may be acceptable when upmarket
entries.body: If small customers churn while larger accounts stay and grow, logo churn can be high but revenue churn low. This is acceptable when the strategy is deliberately moving upmarket — but only if revenue retention holds.

entries.title: Churn > 5%/month is a structural red flag
entries.body: At 5% monthly churn the base halves in ~14 months; acquisition must run constantly just to stand still. Persistent >5% monthly churn usually signals a product-market-fit, pricing, or onboarding problem, not a sales problem.

entries.title: SaaS Quick Ratio — (New + Expansion) ÷ (Churned + Contraction)
entries.body: A ratio above 4 indicates healthy growth efficiency (for every $1 of lost MRR, more than $4 is added). Below 2 suggests the business is treading water. It is a cleaner health signal than top-line growth alone.

entries.title: Strict revenue-churn formula
entries.body: Monthly revenue churn rate = (MRR lost to downgrades + cancellations during the month) ÷ MRR at start of month × 100. Exclude expansion from the numerator; expansion belongs in net-retention, not churn.
